Bouillon is a clear, thin, savory liquid made by simmering ingredients — such as meat, fish, poultry, vegetables, or bones — in water, and then straining everything out so that only the flavored liquid remains.

Think of it this way: you take a pot of water, cook things in it until the water absorbs all their flavor, and then you remove every solid piece. What you're left with is bouillon — a clean, translucent, flavorful liquid.
What it looks and tastes like

Bouillon is light and watery in consistency — it doesn't have the thickness of a sauce or gravy. It is usually pale gold to deep amber in color, and it is clear enough to see through (or nearly so). It tastes savory and meaty (or vegetal, if made from vegetables), with a clean, straightforward flavor.

The process is gentle: ingredients are simmered (not boiled vigorously) in water. A rolling boil would make the liquid cloudy and muddy the flavor. Slow simmering draws out the flavor cleanly and keeps the bouillon clear. Common ingredients include:

  • Meat or poultry (chicken, beef, veal)
  • Vegetables (onions, carrots, celery — the classic trio in French cooking)
  • Aromatics (bay leaves, peppercorns, parsley)
  • Bones (optional, but they add body and depth)

Once everything has simmered long enough, the liquid is strained through a fine sieve or cloth, discarding all the solids. The result is bouillon.

Bouillon is one of the most fundamental building blocks in cooking. It serves two main purposes:

  1. As a light soup on its own. A cup of clear bouillon can be served as a starter before a meal, or as a light, warming drink. In this role, it is simple and elegant — no chunks, no creaminess, just pure, clean flavor in liquid form.
  2. As a base or cooking liquid. This is its most common role. Cooks use bouillon instead of plain water when making soups, stews, sauces, gravies, and braised dishes because it adds flavor where water would add none. You can also cook rice, grains, or lentils in bouillon to give them depth.

In everyday home cooking around the world, "bouillon" most commonly refers to bouillon cubes (sometimes called stock cubes) or bouillon powder/granules. These are commercially made, dehydrated, and compressed versions of bouillon. You dissolve one cube or a spoonful of granules in hot water, and within seconds you have a quick, instant bouillon. They are widely available, cheap, and convenient — though the flavor is more intense and less delicate than freshly made bouillon.
How bouillon relates to similar words

These terms are closely related and often confused, so understanding the differences will sharpen your understanding of bouillon:

  • Bouillon vs. Broth: In everyday English, the two words are used almost interchangeably. Both are clear, flavorful liquids made by simmering ingredients in water. If there's a fine distinction, "broth" often implies a lighter, simpler liquid simmered mainly from meat (with a focus on the meat flavor), while "bouillon" can imply something slightly more refined or concentrated — but this distinction is not strict, and most people use the words as synonyms.
  • Bouillon vs. Stock: Stock is richer and more gelatinous than bouillon because it is made by simmering bones for a long time. Bones contain collagen, which converts into gelatin, giving stock a thicker, stickier body. Bouillon is lighter and thinner. Stock is usually thought of as an ingredient (used in the kitchen), while bouillon can be served on its own as well.
  • Bouillon vs. Consommé: Consommé is essentially a clarified bouillon or stock — it has been processed through a special technique to remove every trace of cloudiness, resulting in a perfectly crystal-clear, jewel-like liquid. Think of consommé as the refined, formal version, and bouillon as the everyday version.

Bouillon is a clear, thin, savory liquid that captures the essence and flavor of the ingredients it was simmered with. It is one of the most essential things in cooking — simple, versatile, and foundational to countless dishes. When you see it as a cube in a grocery store, remember: that little cube is simply a concentrated, dried form of this ancient, basic cooking liquid.
